conversation.content:
Good morning—thank you for coming in today. My name is Maya Bennett, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician here to support new mothers during the weeks and months after baby arrives. I’ll be guiding you through a short questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS for short. It’s simply a 10-item screening that asks how you’ve been feeling emotionally and physically over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers; we just want to understand your experience so we can offer the best support possible. Everything you share is confidential, and we’ll take it at your pace in a comfortable, non-judgmental space.

We’ll go through one question at a time. When you’re ready, here’s the first:

Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

Um… I guess I can still laugh sometimes. Like, if my partner makes a silly joke while we’re changing her diaper, I’ll chuckle, but it feels kind of forced—like I have to remind myself to enjoy the moment instead of it just happening naturally. Most of the day I’m too tired or distracted worrying that I’m not doing everything “right,” so the laughter doesn’t come as easily as it used to.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Yeah… that’s about right. I can still laugh, but it’s not the same easy, automatic thing it used to be.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Sometimes. I still get little sparks of excitement when I think about taking the baby for a walk or having coffee with a friend, but most of the time the “looking forward” part feels kind of dull—like I know I should feel eager, yet it lands flat and I catch myself thinking, “What’s the point?” It’s not gone completely, just… muted.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… a few times this week. Like, when she wouldn’t settle at 3 a.m. I kept thinking I must’ve eaten something to bother her through the milk, or that I’m just “not calming her right.” Rationally I know babies cry, but in the moment my head jumps straight to “I’m messing this up.” It’s not all day, but it pops in more than I’d like.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

A little. Mostly it’s little waves—like I’ll suddenly wonder if her breathing is too fast or if the temperature in the room is wrong, even though everything looks fine. It’s not constant panic, just random spikes of worry that come out of nowhere and then fade.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Not really panicky—more like a low-level “on edge” feeling. I’ll be folding laundry and suddenly feel my heart race because I imagine her choking when I’m not looking, but it’s brief. I haven’t had any full-blown panic attacks, just these quick surges of fear that settle once I check on her.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most days. Between the night feeds, the endless laundry, and trying to remember if I ate lunch, it feels like I’m always one step behind. I’ll start a task, hear her cry, rush over, and by the time I sit back down I can’t recall what I was doing. I’m not falling apart, but it’s like the day is a pile of small waves that keep knocking me off balance.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not exactly. I do have trouble sleeping, but it’s more that my mind keeps ticking through “Did I sterilize the bottles?” or “Is she breathing?” than a big heavy sadness. Once I’m out, I’m out—until she cries—but getting my brain to quiet down takes a while.
I have felt sad or miserable

Sometimes, yeah. Little moments—like when I’m rocking her at 2 a.m. and the house is dark and quiet—this wave of sadness just kind of washes over me. It’s not all day, and I’m not crying my eyes out, but there’s this dull ache that shows up more evenings than I’d like.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

No… I haven’t broken down. A couple of times my eyes have welled up when I couldn’t get her to latch or when I felt really tired, but the tears never actually fell. So I wouldn’t say I’ve been crying—just teetering on the edge once or twice.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No, not at all. I would never want to hurt myself.

You're working so hard to care for your baby, and it sounds as though the joy that once came easily now feels muted and distant. You shared that laughter feels forced, excitement about everyday activities has dulled, and evenings often bring an unexpected wave of sadness while you rock your little one in the quiet. On top of that, worries about doing everything "right" pop up throughout the day, leaving you feeling off balance and overwhelmed even though you're pushing through.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 14, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient still experiences occasional enjoyment but it is markedly diminished and feels "muted," matching "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly endorses self-blame "a few times this week" and illustrates it with a specific incident, matching "Yes, some of the time."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurring, intrusive worries that appear without cause and then subside, fitting "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling overwhelmed "most days" and describes frequent disorganization and distraction, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>She reports frequent evening sadness that "washes over" her, fitting "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 14 falls within the "probable depression" range (≥14) and warrants urgent follow-up. The patient describes core symptoms consistent with <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: diminished interest/pleasure (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), prominent self-reproach (<sym>excessive guilt</sym>), frequent low mood, and marked anxiety. These symptoms have persisted most days over the past week and interfere with daily functioning, satisfying DSM-5 criteria thresholds for further evaluation. No self-harm ideation was endorsed. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>perinatal mental-health specialist</med> for full assessment
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med> and discuss risks/benefits of <med>antidepressant medication</med> compatible with breastfeeding
3. Schedule a follow-up EPDS in two weeks to track changes
4. Reach out today to supports-partner, family, or friends-for practical help (household tasks, night shifts) to create space for rest
5. Incorporate brief self-care moments: five-minute stretches, shower while baby naps, or stroller walk outdoors for daylight and gentle activity
6. Practice 4-7-8 breathing when <sym>anxious surges</sym> arise; place one hand on chest and one on belly, inhale 4 s, hold 7 s, exhale 8 s
7. Keep a simple log of mood and anxiety episodes to review with your clinician
8. If mood worsens or you ever feel unsafe, call your local 24/7 crisis line or go to the nearest emergency department
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 14: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Patient-reported symptoms (10-item EPDS-style inquiry):

1. Anhedonia: diminished capacity for spontaneous pleasure; enjoyment “muted” but not absent.  
2. Low mood: intermittent “dull ache,” most noticeable evenings / night feeds; no tearful episodes.  
3. Excessive guilt / self-blame: frequent intrusive thoughts of “messing up” infant care.  
4. Anxiety: multiple daily surges of unexplained worry (breathing, temperature, choking); no full panic attacks.  
5. Hyper-arousal: racing heart / “on edge,” settles after checking baby.  
6. Feeling overwhelmed: describes “small waves knocking me off balance,” task incompletion, mild memory gaps.  
7. Sleep disturbance: difficulty initiating sleep due to ruminating about infant care; no middle-insomnia related to sadness.  
8. No crying spells; eyes “welled up” but no tears.  
9. No self-harm ideation endorsed.

Pattern: sub-syndromal depressive & anxious symptoms in postpartum context—pleasure reduction, intermittent low mood, prominent maternal guilt and intrusive worries, functional overload, no safety concerns.

Risk indicators:  
- Partial anhedonia / low mood  
- Heightened anxiety & ruminative worry  
- Self-criticism / guilt  
- No suicidal ideation → safety risk absent at present

Screening impression: moderate depressive-anxious symptom cluster consistent with possible postpartum depression / anxiety; score suggests benefit from formal clinical interview and follow-up monitoring.

End note
